title: Fill in the blank: strings
prompt: Fill in the missing piece of code that stores, walks, and changes a string one byte at a time.

blanks.prompt: Store the word yes with no zero byte after it, as a piece that the next string in .data finishes.
blanks.explanation: .ascii stores only the character codes, here 3 bytes. The text that follows it in memory then reads as part of the same string, up to the next zero byte. .string and .asciz would add the zero byte.
blanks.hint: It is the one text directive that adds nothing after the characters.

blanks.prompt: Load the byte at the address in x9 into w10, with the rest of w10 set to zero.
blanks.explanation: ldrb loads a single byte, one character, and fills the rest of w10 with zeros. ldr w10 would load four bytes, four characters at once.
blanks.hint: Add the letter for byte to the load instruction.

blanks.prompt: Store the low byte of w10 at the address in x9, then move x9 on to the next byte.
blanks.explanation: strb stores only the lowest byte of the register, one character. The , 1 after the brackets is post-indexing: the store uses x9 as it is, then adds 1 to it, ready for the next character.
blanks.hint: It is the store that pairs with ldrb.

blanks.prompt: w10 holds the byte that ldrb just loaded from the string. Compare it so that the b.eq walk_done after this line leaves the loop at the byte that ends the string.
blanks.explanation: A string ends at the byte that holds 0. Comparing the loaded byte with 0 and branching when they are equal leaves the loop there. cbz w10, walk_done does the same in one instruction.
blanks.hint: The terminator holds the smallest value a byte can hold.

blanks.prompt: Turn the lower-case letter in w10 into its capital.
blanks.explanation: Each lower-case letter's code is 32 more than its capital's: a is 97 and A is 65. Subtracting 32 turns any lower-case letter into its capital, so the program checks first that w10 holds a letter from a to z.
blanks.hint: Work out the code of a minus the code of A.

blanks.prompt: Load entry 3 of the table of string addresses whose base is in x20.
blanks.explanation: Every entry is an address, 8 bytes, and entries count from 0, so entry 3 starts 3 * 8 = 24 bytes past the base. What comes back in x21 is the address of that string's first byte.
blanks.hint: Multiply the entry number by the size of one address.
